title: King Janaka's Teacher
hookLine: a wandering teacher wins over a king with a hundred teachers, and the king stays king
carry: like Janaka: free while living in the world
tomorrow: a father has his son break open a banyan seed

cards: In the Mahabharata's great book of teachings, King Janaka of Mithila keeps a hundred teachers at his court, each with a different path to offer.
Then a wandering teacher arrives: Panchashikha, a student in the line of the sage Kapila. He sits with the king's scholars and takes on their views one by one.
And Janaka, the story says, sets aside his hundred teachers and follows this one. But he doesn't leave his throne. Janaka stays king.
And in the same book he's remembered for one line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.

teach.b: Panchashikha's line is the one the Samkhya Karika names near its end: the teaching passed from Kapila to Asuri, from Asuri to Panchashikha, and down a line of students to Ishvarakrishna, who set it in these verses.
And the Karika takes on the hardest question Janaka's court could ask. Purusha never acts. It doesn't think or move.
So how could anyone know it's there?

teach.h: WHAT'S PUT TOGETHER IS FOR ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Karika's first reason is homely: whatever is put together exists for someone else.
Commentators make it concrete with a bed: frame, slats, mattress, all fitted together, and plainly for a sleeper who isn't one of the parts.
Now look at a body and a mind, all fitted together. For whom?

The verse adds more: there must be something beyond the three gunas, someone to oversee it all, someone who experiences it; and people strive for release, which makes no sense unless someone is there to be freed.
Samkhya can't point at purusha. It infers it, the way you'd infer a sleeper from a made bed. Then Janaka shows what the knowing is for.
Hindus hold him up as the householder sage, free while ruling a city, and the Bhagavad Gita names him: Janaka and others reached perfection through action.

teach.h: FREE WHILE LIVING IN THE WORLD.
teach.b: So in Hindu teaching, you don't have to leave home for the forest to be free. A job, a family and a full calendar aren't in the way. They're the bed.

how: The Samkhya Karika is read verse by verse with classical commentaries such as Gaudapada's, and its arguments, like the one for purusha, are studied alongside other schools' replies. Janaka is held up in Hindu teaching as the model of a householder who seeks freedom without leaving the world.

s: Samkhya says you can see purusha directly, like any object
purusha never acts or appears; the Karika infers it with reasons.
the Karika argues that whatever is put together exists for another
commentators picture a bed, made of parts, for a sleeper outside them.
Janaka gave up his kingdom to follow Panchashikha

games.q: you're a Samkhya teacher at Janaka's court. a scholar says: purusha never thinks or moves, so how could anyone know it's there?
o: you can't; it's just a belief.
reason it out: what's put together is for someone outside it.
games.why: the Karika infers purusha: assemblies exist for another, there must be an experiencer, and people strive for release.

practice: Notice the arrangement you are right now: the spine holding you up, the lungs filling, the heart keeping time, the ears taking in the room. Feel the whole assembly at once, and rest in the plain fact that it's being experienced.

Then think of one duty waiting for you today, and plan to do it the way Janaka ruled: fully, without being owned by it. If you pray, give thanks for the body that's been made, and offer the day's work in your own words.

wordCard.voice: The Samkhya Karika. Ishvarakrishna's verses, from Kapila's line, which reason that whatever is put together, like a bed, is for someone outside it: purusha.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Ishvarakrishna's book of verses on Samkhya.

carryVoice: Your line: like Janaka, free while living in the world. A made bed points to its sleeper. That's the week.
